misconception.description: adding the after-tax profit target to the fixed costs without first grossing it up to the pre-tax profit that produces it

worked_example.text: A pottery studio has fixed costs of EUR 30,000 a year. A workshop place sells for EUR 120 and costs EUR 45 in clay, glaze and firing. The studio pays tax at 25% and its owner wants EUR 15,000 of profit after tax.
worked_example.solution: Pre-tax profit needed = 15,000 / 0.75 = EUR 20,000. Margin = 120 - 45 = EUR 75. Places = (30,000 + 20,000) / 75 = 666.67, so 667 places.

problem.text: A training studio has fixed costs of EUR 96,000 a year. A course sells for EUR 400 and costs EUR 160 to run. The studio pays tax at 20% on its profits and wants to earn EUR 48,000 after tax. How many courses must it sell?

distractors.note: the documented misconception: the after-tax target treated as if it were pre-tax
multiplying by one minus the tax rate instead of dividing, shrinking the target rather than grossing it up

hints: Tax is charged on the profit the studio earns, so the figure that drives sales volume is the profit before tax, not the amount the owner ends up keeping.
If the tax authority takes a fifth of the pre-tax profit, then what the owner keeps is four fifths of it. Recover the pre-tax figure by dividing the target by one minus the tax rate.
Treat that pre-tax profit as though it were an extra fixed cost: add it to the EUR 96,000 and divide the total by the margin on one course.
worked_solution: Step 1: gross up the target. At a 20% tax rate the owner keeps 80% of the pre-tax profit, so 48,000 / 0.8 = EUR 60,000 has to be earned before tax. Step 2: the margin on a course is 400 - 160 = EUR 240. Step 3: the courses must cover the fixed costs and that pre-tax profit: (96,000 + 60,000) / 240 = 650 courses. Adding the after-tax target straight to the fixed costs would give 600 courses, and at that volume the tax bill leaves the owner with only EUR 38,400.

near_transfer.text: The same training studio, with EUR 96,000 of fixed costs, a EUR 400 price, a EUR 160 variable cost and a 20% tax rate, sells 800 courses in the year. What profit does it make after tax?

distractors.note: reporting the pre-tax profit as if it were what the owner keeps
grossing up a figure that should instead be taxed down

far_transfer.text: A workshop plans to sell 1,000 units next year. Its fixed costs are EUR 120,000, each unit costs EUR 90 to make and it pays tax at 20%. What price must it charge to earn EUR 96,000 after tax?

distractors.note: the misconception: no gross-up of the after-tax target
forgetting to add back what each unit costs to make
